row.name: North Ridge (from Culebra Peak)
row.description: Reached only across private ranch land with a permit; it is a ridge walk usually done after Culebra Peak.

row.name: Southeast Ridge
row.description: Open ridge and loose talus above Telluride's Ophir area with a short final scramble.

row.name: North Ridge
row.description: Rocky ridge scramble that is usually combined with French Mountain and Frasco Benchmark.

row.name: South Ridge and Slopes
row.description: Remote tundra walk reached by a rough road near Creede; adds a few miles if the road is not driven.

row.name: East Slopes from Meysan Lake
row.description: Hike the Meysan Lakes trail to the lake, then climb the loose gully near the south side of the east ridge to the plateau and the summit blocks. Scree and talus all the way.

row.name: Stone Meysan
row.overview: On a buttress partway between Irvine and Mallory, the route climbs four long pitches of corners and faces, then bends sideways into a few rope lengths of ridge climbing. P1: base of a corner, loose ledges and a blocky crack. P2: discontinuous cracks to a blocky stance. P3: left, over a small roof, into the main corner. P4: corner to the top. P5-7: blocky ridge, class 3 up to easy fifth class. Afterward walk southward on the divide and drop to Meysan Lake by way of Green Pass's East Slopes.
row.approach: Start at the Meysan Lakes trailhead by the Whitney Portal campground and follow that trail to the head of the drainage; overnight stays need a permit. The route sits on a nameless buttress on the hillside between Mt. Irvine and Mt. Mallory, above Meysan Lake. A short walk up boulders and talus from the lake leads into the gully below the wall.
row.descent_text: The route finishes with a blocky ridge of third to low fifth class that ends on the Irvine-Mallory divide. Hike south along the divide, then drop to Meysan Lake by the east slopes of Green Pass.

row.name: Via Arc Pass
row.description: Reach Arc Pass, then climb scree and talus to the south summit. Downclimb a class 3 step into the notch, go up a short way and follow a ramp left onto easy scrambling to the highest point. Exposed; a rope may be welcome.

row.name: NE Ridge (full)
row.overview: Visible from Lone Pine, this is the middle one of three prominent ridges. The complete traverse covers 3 miles and gains 6900 feet, and many parties need multiple days. No water is available on the ridge, though the descent may have some depending on season. The rock is often friable, in contrast to the N Ridge, but the hard parts are short and routefinding is moderate. Nothing harder than 5.6 was found on the original line, though 5.7 is also reported. The hardest part may be the vague, bushy E ledges descent.
row.approach: The ridge is reached from Olivas Ranch Road on the edge of Lone Pine. From the end of that road, take the faint trail to the stream, cross it, and climb the right-hand skyline ridge on sandy class 2 ground until the rock steps begin. A nicer parking area exists at the base of the route, off the Lone Pine campground road. The full ridge is long and has no water on it, so many parties take more than one day.
row.descent_text: Two descents are used. The east ledges descent goes down the sandy class 2 slopes with the east ridgeline in view, avoiding the steep cliffs to the south and southeast by contouring left whenever they feel close. Expect no trail or cairns, a ridge that forks several times, and loose, brushy ground in the gully; it leads to the Tuttle Creek road, and a few miles of road walking return you to the Olivas Ranch Road turnaround. The alternative is the class 2 west side of the peak into the Meysan Lakes cirque, then the Meysan Lakes trail past the summer cabins to the Lone Pine campground or a nearby dirt road. Cutting across to a more direct gully can involve a short class 5 chimney, so the longer walk is the safer choice.

row.name: SouthEast ridge Direct
row.overview: Roughly 1000 feet of ridge scrambling and climbing northwest to the summit over boulders and gendarmes; stay close to the crest and finish over an overhanging bulge. Hard moves are short and many can be avoided, but never ascend what you cannot reverse. The simplest place to begin is the major notch in the ridge (big tower on the right, narrow one on the left); about 400 feet lower southeast adds more climbing. From Whitney Portal the approach to the notch is +4950 ft over 4.5 miles. Descend by scrambling down the south or southwest side to talus and sand, then hike south to the approach. A wilderness permit from the USFS is required.
